1 --- 2 name: visual-explainer 3 description: Generate beautiful, self-contained HTML pages that visually explain systems, code changes, plans, and data. Use when the user asks for a diagram, architecture overview, diff review, plan review, project recap, comparison table, or any visual explanation of technical concepts. Also use proactively when you are about to render a complex ASCII table (4+ rows or 3+ columns) — present it as a styled HTML page instead. 4 license: MIT 5 compatibility: Requires a browser to view generated HTML files. Optional surf-cli for AI image generation. 6 metadata: 7 author: nicobailon 8 version: "0.6.3" 9 --- 10 11 # Visual Explainer 12 13 Generate self-contained HTML files for technical diagrams, visualizations, and data tables. Always open the result in the browser. Never fall back to ASCII art when this skill is loaded. 14 15 **Proactive table rendering.** When you're about to present tabular data as an ASCII box-drawing table in the terminal (comparisons, audits, feature matrices, status reports, any structured rows/columns), generate an HTML page instead. The threshold: if the table has 4+ rows or 3+ columns, it belongs in the browser. Don't wait for the user to ask — render it as HTML automatically and tell them the file path. You can still include a brief text summary in the chat, but the table itself should be the HTML page. 16 17 ## Available Commands 18 19 Detailed prompt templates in `./commands/`. In Pi, these are slash commands (`/diff-review`). In Claude Code, namespaced (`/visual-explainer:diff-review`). In Codex, use `/prompts:diff-review` (if installed to `~/.codex/prompts/`) or invoke `$visual-explainer` and describe the workflow. 20 21 | Command | What it does | 22 |---------|-------------| 23 | `generate-web-diagram` | Generate an HTML diagram for any topic | 24 | `generate-visual-plan` | Generate a visual implementation plan for a feature | 25 | `generate-slides` | Generate a magazine-quality slide deck | 26 | `diff-review` | Visual diff review with architecture comparison and code review | 27 | `plan-review` | Compare a plan against the codebase with risk assessment | 28 | `project-recap` | Mental model snapshot for context-switching back to a project | 29 | `fact-check` | Verify accuracy of a document against actual code | 30 | `share` | Deploy an HTML page to Vercel and get a live URL | 31 32 ## Workflow 33 34 ### 1. Think (5 seconds, not 5 minutes) 35 36 Before writing HTML, commit to a direction. Don't default to "dark theme with blue accents" every time. 37 38 **Visual is always default.** Even essays, blog posts, and articles get visual treatment — extract structure into cards, diagrams, grids, tables. 39 40 Prose patterns (lead paragraphs, pull quotes, callout boxes) are **accent elements** within visual pages, not a separate mode. Use them to highlight key points or provide breathing room, but the page structure remains visual. 41 42 For prose accents, see "Prose Page Elements" in `./references/css-patterns.md`. For everything else, use the standard freeform approach with aesthetic directions below. 43 44 **Who is looking?** A developer understanding a system? A PM seeing the big picture? A team reviewing a proposal? This shapes information density and visual complexity. 45 46 **What type of content?** Architecture, flowchart, sequence, data flow, schema/ER, state machine, mind map, class diagram, C4 architecture, data table, timeline, dashboard, or prose-first page. Each has distinct layout needs and rendering approaches (see Diagram Types below). 47 48 **What aesthetic?** Pick one and commit. The constrained aesthetics (Blueprint, Editorial, Paper/ink) are safer — they have specific requirements that prevent generic output. The flexible ones (IDE-inspired) require more discipline. 49 50 **Constrained aesthetics (prefer these):** 51 - Blueprint (technical drawing feel, subtle grid background, deep slate/blue palette, monospace labels, precise borders) — see `websocket-implementation-plan.html` for reference 52 - Editorial (serif headlines like Instrument Serif or Crimson Pro, generous whitespace, muted earth tones or deep navy + gold) 53 - Paper/ink (warm cream `#faf7f5` background, terracotta/sage accents, informal feel) 54 - Monochrome terminal (green/amber on near-black, monospace everything, CRT glow optional) 55 56 **Flexible aesthetics (use with caution):** 57 - IDE-inspired (borrow a real, named color scheme: Dracula, Nord, Catppuccin Mocha/Latte, Solarized Dark/Light, Gruvbox, One Dark, Rosé Pine) — commit to the actual palette, don't approximate 58 - Data-dense (small type, tight spacing, maximum information, muted colors) 59 60 **Explicitly forbidden:** 61 - Neon dashboard (cyan + magenta + purple on dark) — always produces AI slop 62 - Gradient mesh (pink/purple/cyan blobs) — too generic 63 - Any combination of Inter font + violet/indigo accents + gradient text 64 65 Vary the choice each time. If the last diagram was dark and technical, make the next one light and editorial. The swap test: if you replaced your styling with a generic dark theme and nobody would notice the difference, you haven't designed anything. 66 67 ### 2. Structure 68 69 **Read the reference material** before generating. Don't memorize it — read it each time to absorb the patterns. 70 - For text-heavy architecture overviews (card content matters more than topology): read `./templates/architecture.html` 71 - For flowcharts, sequence diagrams, ER, state machines, mind maps, class diagrams, C4: read `./templates/mermaid-flowchart.html` 72 - For data tables, comparisons, audits, feature matrices: read `./templates/data-table.html` 73 - For slide deck presentations (when `--slides` flag is present or `/generate-slides` is invoked): read `./templates/slide-deck.html` and `./references/slide-patterns.md` 74 - For prose-heavy publishable pages (READMEs, articles, blog posts, essays): read the "Prose Page Elements" section in `./references/css-patterns.md` and "Typography by Content Voice" in `./references/libraries.md` 75 76 **For CSS/layout patterns and SVG connectors**, read `./references/css-patterns.md`. 77 78 **For pages with 4+ sections** (reviews, recaps, dashboards), also read `./references/responsive-nav.md` for section navigation with sticky sidebar TOC on desktop and horizontal scrollable bar on mobile. 79 80 **Choosing a rendering approach:** 81 82 | Content type | Approach | Why | 83 |---|---|---| 84 | Architecture (text-heavy) | CSS Grid cards + flow arrows | Rich card content (descriptions, code, tool lists) needs CSS control | 85 | Architecture (topology-focused) | **Mermaid** | Visible connections between components need automatic edge routing | 86 | Flowchart / pipeline | **Mermaid** | Automatic node positioning and edge routing | 87 | Sequence diagram | **Mermaid** | Lifelines, messages, and activation boxes need automatic layout | 88 | Data flow | **Mermaid** with edge labels | Connections and data descriptions need automatic edge routing | 89 | ER / schema diagram | **Mermaid** | Relationship lines between many entities need auto-routing | 90 | State machine | **Mermaid** | State transitions with labeled edges need automatic layout | 91 | Mind map | **Mermaid** | Hierarchical branching needs automatic positioning | 92 | Class diagram | **Mermaid** | Inheritance, composition, aggregation lines with automatic routing | 93 | C4 architecture | **Mermaid** | Use `graph TD` + `subgraph` for C4 (not native `C4Context` — it ignores themes) | 94 | Data table | HTML `` | Semantic markup, accessibility, copy-paste behavior | 95 | Timeline | CSS (central line + cards) | Simple linear layout doesn't need a layout engine | 96 | Dashboard | CSS Grid + Chart.js | Card grid with embedded charts | 97 98 **Mermaid theming:** Always use `theme: 'base'` with custom `themeVariables` so colors match your page palette. Use `layout: 'elk'` for complex graphs (requires the `@mermaid-js/layout-elk` package — see `./references/libraries.md` for the CDN import). Override Mermaid's SVG classes with CSS for pixel-perfect control. See `./references/libraries.md` for full theming guide. 99 100 **Mermaid containers:** Always center Mermaid diagrams with `display: flex; justify-content: center;`. Add zoom controls (+/−/reset/expand) to every `.mermaid-wrap` container. Include the click-to-expand JavaScript so clicking the diagram (or the ⛶ button) opens it full-size in a new tab. 101 102 **⚠️ Never use bare `
`.** It renders but has no zoom/pan controls — diagrams become tiny and unusable. Always use the full `diagram-shell` pattern from `templates/mermaid-flowchart.html`: the HTML structure (`.diagram-shell` > `.mermaid-wrap` > `.zoom-controls` + `.mermaid-viewport` > `.mermaid-canvas`), the CSS, and the ~200-line JS module for zoom/pan/fit. Copy it wholesale.
   103	
   104	**Mermaid scaling:** Diagrams with 10+ nodes render too small by default. For 10-12 nodes, increase `fontSize` in themeVariables to 18-20px and set `INITIAL_ZOOM` to 1.5-1.6. For 15+ elements, don't try to scale — use the hybrid pattern instead (simple Mermaid overview + CSS Grid cards). See "Architecture / System Diagrams" below.
   105	
   106	**Mermaid layout direction:** Prefer `flowchart TD` (top-down) over `flowchart LR` (left-to-right) for complex diagrams. LR spreads horizontally and makes labels unreadable when there are many nodes. Use LR only for simple 3-4 node linear flows. See `./references/libraries.md` "Layout Direction: TD vs LR".
   107	
   108	**Mermaid line breaks in flowchart labels:** Use `
` inside quoted labels. Never use escaped newlines like `\n` (Mermaid renders them as literal text in HTML output). Example: `A["Copilot Backend
/api + /api/voicebot"]`.
   109	
   110	**Mermaid CSS class collision constraint:** Never define `.node` as a page-level CSS class. Mermaid.js uses `.node` internally on SVG `` elements with `transform: translate(x, y)` for positioning. Page-level `.node` styles (hover transforms, box-shadows) leak into diagrams and break layout. Use the namespaced `.ve-card` class for card components instead. The only safe way to style Mermaid's `.node` is scoped under `.mermaid` (e.g., `.mermaid .node rect`).
   111	
   112	**AI-generated illustrations (optional).** If [surf-cli](https://github.com/nicobailon/surf-cli) is available, you can generate images via Gemini and embed them in the page for creative, illustrative, explanatory, educational, or decorative purposes. Check availability with `which surf`. If available:
   113	
   114	```bash
   115	# Generate to a temp file (use --aspect-ratio for control)
   116	surf gemini "descriptive prompt" --generate-image /tmp/ve-img.png --aspect-ratio 16:9
   117	
   118	# Base64 encode for self-containment (macOS)
   119	IMG=$(base64 -i /tmp/ve-img.png)
   120	# Linux: IMG=$(base64 -w 0 /tmp/ve-img.png)
   121	
   122	# Embed in HTML and clean up
   123	# 
   124	rm /tmp/ve-img.png
   125	```
   126	
   127	See `./references/css-patterns.md` for image container styles (hero banners, inline illustrations, captions).
   128	
   129	**When to use:** Hero banners that establish the page's visual tone. Conceptual illustrations for abstract systems that Mermaid can't express (physical infrastructure, user journeys, mental models). Educational diagrams that benefit from artistic or photorealistic rendering. Decorative accents that reinforce the aesthetic.
   130	
   131	**When to skip:** Anything Mermaid or CSS handles well. Generic decoration that doesn't convey meaning. Data-heavy pages where images would distract. Always degrade gracefully — if surf isn't available, skip images without erroring. The page should stand on its own with CSS and typography alone.
   132	
   133	**Prompt craft:** Match the image to the page's palette and aesthetic direction. Specify the style (3D render, technical illustration, watercolor, isometric, flat vector, etc.) and mention dominant colors from your CSS variables. Use `--aspect-ratio 16:9` for hero banners, `--aspect-ratio 1:1` for inline illustrations. Keep prompts specific — "isometric illustration of a message queue with cyan nodes on dark navy background" beats "a diagram of a queue."
   134	
   135	### 3. Style
   136	
   137	Apply these principles to every diagram:
   138	
   139	**Typography is the diagram.** Pick a distinctive font pairing from the list in `./references/libraries.md`. Every page should use a different pairing from recent generations.
   140	
   141	**Forbidden as `--font-body`:** Inter, Roboto, Arial, Helvetica, system-ui alone. These are AI slop signals.
   142	
   143	**Good pairings (use these):**
   144	- DM Sans + Fira Code (technical, precise)
   145	- Instrument Serif + JetBrains Mono (editorial, refined)
   146	- IBM Plex Sans + IBM Plex Mono (reliable, readable)
   147	- Bricolage Grotesque + Fragment Mono (bold, characterful)
   148	- Plus Jakarta Sans + Azeret Mono (rounded, approachable)
   149	
   150	Load via `` in ``. Include a system font fallback in the `font-family` stack for offline resilience.
   151	
   152	**Color tells a story.** Use CSS custom properties for the full palette. Define at minimum: `--bg`, `--surface`, `--border`, `--text`, `--text-dim`, and 3-5 accent colors. Each accent should have a full and a dim variant (for backgrounds). Name variables semantically when possible (`--pipeline-step` not `--blue-3`). Support both themes.
   153	
   154	**Forbidden accent colors:** `#8b5cf6` `#7c3aed` `#a78bfa` (indigo/violet), `#d946ef` (fuchsia), the cyan-magenta-pink combination. These are Tailwind defaults that signal zero design intent.
   155	
   156	**Good accent palettes (use these):**
   157	- Terracotta + sage (`#c2410c`, `#65a30d`) — warm, earthy
   158	- Teal + slate (`#0891b2`, `#0369a1`) — technical, precise
   159	- Rose + cranberry (`#be123c`, `#881337`) — editorial, refined
   160	- Amber + emerald (`#d97706`, `#059669`) — data-focused
   161	- Deep blue + gold (`#1e3a5f`, `#d4a73a`) — premium, sophisticated
   162	
   163	Put your primary aesthetic in `:root` and the alternate in the media query:
   164	
   165	```css
   166	/* Light-first (editorial, paper/ink, blueprint): */
   167	:root { /* light values */ }
   168	@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root { /* dark values */ } }
   169	
   170	/* Dark-first (neon, IDE-inspired, terminal): */
   171	:root { /* dark values */ }
   172	@media (prefers-color-scheme: light) { :root { /* light values */ } }
   173	```
   174	
   175	**Surfaces whisper, they don't shout.** Build depth through subtle lightness shifts (2-4% between levels), not dramatic color changes. Borders should be low-opacity rgba (`rgba(255,255,255,0.08)` in dark mode, `rgba(0,0,0,0.08)` in light) — visible when you look, invisible when you don't.
   176	
   177	**Backgrounds create atmosphere.** Don't use flat solid colors for the page background. Subtle gradients, faint grid patterns via CSS, or gentle radial glows behind focal areas. The background should feel like a space, not a void.
   178	
   179	**Visual weight signals importance.** Not every section deserves equal visual treatment. Executive summaries and key metrics should dominate the viewport on load (larger type, more padding, subtle accent-tinted background zone). Reference sections (file maps, dependency lists, decision logs) should be compact and stay out of the way. Use `
/` for sections that are useful but not primary — the collapsible pattern is in `./references/css-patterns.md`.
   180	
   181	**Surface depth creates hierarchy.** Vary card depth to signal what matters. Hero sections get elevated shadows and accent-tinted backgrounds (`ve-card--hero` pattern). Body content stays flat (default `.ve-card`). Code blocks and secondary content feel recessed (`ve-card--recessed`). See the depth tiers in `./references/css-patterns.md`. Don't make everything elevated — when everything pops, nothing does.
   182	
   183	**Animation earns its place.** Staggered fade-ins on page load are almost always worth it — they guide the eye through the diagram's hierarchy. For complex architectures (15+ elements), use the **hybrid pattern**: a simple 5-8 node Mermaid overview showing module relationships, followed by CSS Grid cards with detailed function lists.  3. Uses an editorial color palette (deep navy + gold/amber accents, serif typography feel)

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches
import json
from datetime import datetime
import numpy as np

# Load data
with open('/app/benchmark/source_data.json', 'r') as f:
    data = json.load(f)

# Editorial color palette
COLORS = {
    'research': '#2E5AAC',      # deep blue
    'industry': '#C7891B',      # warm gold/amber
    'regulation': '#2D7D5F',    # forest green
    'investment': '#8B5A3C',    # muted terracotta/brown
    'critical': '#B91C1C',      # deep red for critical events
    'bg': '#FDFCF8',            # warm off-white
    'grid': '#E8E4DE',          # warm gray
    'text': '#1C1C1C',          # near black
    'text_dim': '#6B6560',      # warm gray text
    'highlight': '#C7891B33',   # translucent gold for ChatGPT band
}

# Parse milestone dates
def parse_date(d):
    return datetime.strptime(d, '%Y-%m')

research = [(parse_date(e['date']), e['label'], e['significance']) for e in data['research_milestones']['data']]
industry = [(parse_date(e['date']), e['label'], e['significance']) for e in data['industry_milestones']['data']]
regulation = [(parse_date(e['date']), e['label'], e['significance']) for e in data['regulation_milestones']['data']]

# Investment data
inv_years = [d['year'] for d in data['ai_investment']['data']]
inv_values = [d['investment'] for d in data['ai_investment']['data']]

# Create figure
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(18, 11), facecolor=COLORS['bg'])
ax.set_facecolor(COLORS['bg'])

# Define track positions
tracks = {
    'Research': {'y': 3.2, 'color': COLORS['research'], 'data': research},
    'Industry': {'y': 2.0, 'color': COLORS['industry'], 'data': industry},
    'Regulation': {'y': 0.8, 'color': COLORS['regulation'], 'data': regulation},
}

# Plot investment as area chart in background (bottom portion)
# Map years to x positions (dummy x for area fill)
min_year = 2010
max_year = 2025
years = np.array(inv_years)
values = np.array(inv_values)

# Normalize investment values to fit in the bottom area (0 to 0.6)
max_inv = max(values)
inv_scaled = (values / max_inv) * 0.55

for i in range(len(years) - 1):
    x_vals = [years[i], years[i+1], years[i+1], years[i]]
    y_vals = [0, 0, inv_scaled[i+1], inv_scaled[i]]
    ax.fill(x_vals, y_vals, color=COLORS['investment'], alpha=0.18, zorder=0)

# Add investment line on top
ax.plot(years, inv_scaled, color=COLORS['investment'], linewidth=2.5, alpha=0.8, zorder=1)

# Add investment labels for key years
for year, val in zip(years, values):
    scaled = (val / max_inv) * 0.55
    if year in [2010, 2017, 2022, 2024, 2025]:
        ax.annotate(f'${val:.0f}B', (year, scaled), textcoords="offset points",
                    xytext=(0, 10), fontsize=8, ha='center', color=COLORS['investment'],
                    fontweight='bold', zorder=2)

# Track base lines
for name, info in tracks.items():
    ax.hlines(info['y'], min_year, max_year, colors=info['color'], linewidth=2, alpha=0.4, zorder=2)
    # Track label
    ax.text(min_year - 0.8, info['y'], name, fontsize=11, fontweight='bold',
            color=info['color'], ha='right', va='center', 
            fontfamily='sans-serif')

# Event markers
marker_sizes = {'medium': 60, 'high': 100, 'critical': 160}

for name, info in tracks.items():
    y = info['y']
    color = info['color']
    for date, label, sig in info['data']:
        x = date.year + (date.month - 1) / 12
        size = marker_sizes.get(sig, 80)
        # Outer glow for critical
        if sig == 'critical':
            ax.scatter(x, y, s=size*1.8, c=color, alpha=0.15, zorder=3)
        ax.scatter(x, y, s=size, c=color, edgecolors='white', linewidths=1.5,
                   alpha=0.92, zorder=4)
        
        # Label positioning — alternate above/below to reduce overlap
        idx = info['data'].index((date, label, sig))
        total = len(info['data'])
        # Smart offset: split into two vertical groups
        if idx % 2 == 0:
            y_offset = 28
            va = 'bottom'
        else:
            y_offset = -28
            va = 'top'
        
        fontsize = 7.5 if sig == 'medium' else 8.5
        fontweight = 'bold' if sig == 'critical' else 'normal'
        
        ax.annotate(label, (x, y), textcoords="offset points",
                    xytext=(0, y_offset), fontsize=fontsize, ha='center', va=va,
                    color=COLORS['text'], fontweight=fontweight, zorder=5,
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.25', facecolor=COLORS['bg'],
                              edgecolor='none', alpha=0.85))

# ChatGPT inflection highlight band (Nov 2022)
chatgpt_date = 2022 + 10/12
ax.axvspan(chatgpt_date - 0.25, chatgpt_date + 0.25, ymin=0.72, ymax=1.0,
           facecolor=COLORS['highlight'], edgecolor=COLORS['industry'],
           linewidth=2, linestyle='--', zorder=1)
ax.annotate('ChatGPT\nNov 2022', (chatgpt_date, 3.55), fontsize=9, ha='center',
            va='center', color=COLORS['industry'], fontweight='bold',
            bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.3', facecolor='#FFF8E7', edgecolor=COLORS['industry'], linewidth=1.5))

# Density annotation — compare 2010-2017 vs 2023-2024
ax.annotate('', xy=(2023.5, 3.9), xytext=(2013.5, 3.9),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=COLORS['text_dim'], lw=1.5, ls='--'))
ax.text(2013.5, 4.05, '2010-2017: 13 events', fontsize=8, color=COLORS['text_dim'], ha='left')
ax.text(2023.5, 4.05, '2023-2024: 17 events', fontsize=8, color=COLORS['industry'], ha='right', fontweight='bold')

# Lag pattern annotation
ax.annotate('Research → Industry: 2-4yr lag\nIndustry → Regulation: 3-5yr lag',
            xy=(2016, 0.15), fontsize=8.5, color=COLORS['text_dim'], ha='left',
            style='italic',
            bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.4', facecolor='#F5F3EF', edgecolor=COLORS['grid'], linewidth=1))

# Axis setup
ax.set_xlim(2009, 2026.5)
ax.set_ylim(-0.1, 4.3)
ax.set_xlabel('Year', fontsize=12, color=COLORS['text'], fontweight='bold', labelpad=12)
ax.set_xticks(range(2010, 2026, 2))
ax.tick_params(axis='x', colors=COLORS['text_dim'], labelsize=10)
ax.tick_params(axis='y', left=False, labelleft=False)

# Grid
ax.grid(axis='x', color=COLORS['grid'], linewidth=0.8, linestyle='-', alpha=0.7, zorder=0)
ax.set_axisbelow(True)

# Remove top/right spines
for spine in ['top', 'right']:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
for spine in ['bottom', 'left']:
    ax.spines[spine].set_color(COLORS['grid'])

# Title
ax.set_title('AI Evolution: Three Parallel Tracks (2010–2025)\nwith Global Private Investment Overlay',
             fontsize=16, fontweight='bold', color=COLORS['text'], pad=20,
             fontfamily='serif')

# Legend
legend_elements = [
    mpatches.Patch(facecolor=COLORS['research'], label='Research Milestones'),
    mpatches.Patch(facecolor=COLORS['industry'], label='Industry Milestones'),
    mpatches.Patch(facecolor=COLORS['regulation'], label='Regulation Milestones'),
    mpatches.Patch(facecolor=COLORS['investment'], alpha=0.4, label='AI Investment ($B)'),
]
ax.legend(handles=legend_elements, loc='upper left', frameon=True,
          facecolor=COLORS['bg'], edgecolor=COLORS['grid'], fontsize=9,
          title='Tracks & Overlay', title_fontsize=10)

# Source note
fig.text(0.99, 0.01, 'Data: source_data.json  •  Investment in billions USD',
         fontsize=7, color=COLORS['text_dim'], ha='right', va='bottom', style='italic')

plt.tight_layout(rect=[0.02, 0.03, 1, 0.97])
plt.savefig('/app/output/result.png', dpi=200, facecolor=COLORS['bg'],
            bbox_inches='tight', pad_inches=0.3)
print('Saved /app/output/result.png')
